abstract: Functional characterization of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) is essential for understanding developmental gene regulation and interpreting human noncoding variation. However, conventional transgenesis assays are limited by integration copy number variability and genomic position effects, while species-specific developmental differences constrain the study of human regulatory sequences in classical model organisms, demanding assays based on human-specific contexts. Here, we developed RepoV, a transgenesis vector enabling single-copy integration of enhancer reporter constructs in the genome of human iPS cells through PhiC31-mediated recombination. Transgenic iPSCs were subsequently used to assess candidate neurodevelopmental enhancers in neural organoids. RepoV recapitulated the expected activity of previously characterized regulatory elements and enabled the evaluation of candidate sequences associated with the neurodevelopmental genes POU3F2 and FOXG1. Notably, two FOXG1 enhancers displayed different activities in zebrafish larvae and human neural organoids. The organoid results were more consistent with endogenous the FOXG1 expression and the pathological phenotypes associated with disease-related regulatory variants identified in patients. Together, these findings establish RepoV transgenesis combined with human organoid cultures as a valuable platform for the functional evaluation of human developmental regulatory sequences.
